blocks.text: 1. Human Evaluation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448058794-476910356.png

Hallucination Detection closed by weighing when its dedicated invented-claim checking is worth the added cost. Human Evaluation, real people judging RAG system outputs the automated metrics cannot fully capture, steps back from every automated proxy this module has built to ask what only a human reviewer can actually judge.
Human evaluation has a reviewer read the answer, the context, and the question, then rate what automated checks alone miss.
2. Every Metric So Far Has Been An Automated Proxy

blocks.alt: Every Metric So Far Has Been An Automated Proxy
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448058796-981471325.png
Precision, recall, faithfulness, relevancy, and hallucination detection all use automated models to approximate a judgment.
Every one of those automated judges can itself be wrong in ways a careful human reviewer would not be.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Evaluation type","Who or what makes the judgment"],"rows":[["Automated metrics","A model approximating a judgment"],["Human evaluation","A real person making the judgment directly"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Humans Catch Quality Dimensions Metrics Miss

blocks.alt: Humans Catch Quality Dimensions Metrics Miss
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448058797-603013170.png
Tone, helpfulness, and appropriateness are hard to reduce to a single automated score, much like faithfulness alone does not check factual accuracy.
A human reviewer can judge these dimensions directly, in a way automated metrics were never designed to.
4. Structured Rating Scales Make Human Judgment Comparable

blocks.alt: Structured Rating Scales Make Human Judgment Comparable
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448058797-307902358.png
An unstructured human opinion is hard to aggregate across many reviewers.
A defined rating scale, applied consistently, turns individual opinions into comparable data.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A rating scale like one to five for helpfulness, defined with clear criteria for each number, lets ratings from different reviewers be averaged and compared meaningfully, unlike free-form written opinions alone.

blocks.text: 5. Inter-Rater Reliability Checks Consistency
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448058797-387960281.png
Different human reviewers can disagree on the same answer.
Measuring how often reviewers agree reveals whether the rating scale itself is well defined.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Agreement level","What it suggests"],"rows":[["High inter-rater agreement","Rating scale and criteria are well defined"],["Low inter-rater agreement","Rating scale needs clearer criteria"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Human Evaluation Is Slow And Expensive

blocks.alt: Human Evaluation Is Slow And Expensive
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448058797-828122734.png
A human reviewing each answer takes real time per query, far more than any automated metric requires.
Human evaluation does not scale to every query in a large evaluation set.
7. Human Evaluation Validates Automated Metrics
Comparing human ratings against automated scores on the same sample reveals whether the automated metric actually tracks what matters.
A mismatch between the two signals that the automated metric needs adjustment.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: An automated faithfulness score consistently disagreeing with human ratings on the same sample of answers signals that the automated judge model itself needs tuning, not just the RAG system being evaluated.

blocks.text: 8. Sampling Strategy For Human Review
Because human evaluation is slow and expensive, a small, representative sample gets reviewed by humans instead of the entire evaluation set.
The sample's results are then generalized back to the system as a whole.
9. Recognizing When Human Evaluation Is Worth Its Cost

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Human Evaluation Is Worth Its Cost
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448058798-931116864.png
Periodically validating that automated metrics still track real quality justifies human evaluation.
Routine, continuous monitoring at scale, by contrast, relies on automated metrics rather than human review.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Relying only on automated metrics without ever validating them against human judgment.
Using an unstructured, free-form rating process that cannot be meaningfully aggregated.
Skipping inter-rater reliability checks and trusting a single reviewer's opinion as ground truth.
Attempting to human-review every query in a large evaluation set instead of a representative sample.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Human evaluation uses real people to judge what automated metrics cannot fully capture.
Every automated metric in this module is a proxy judgment, itself capable of being wrong.
Humans can directly judge tone, helpfulness, and appropriateness in ways automated scores cannot.
A structured, consistently applied rating scale turns individual opinions into comparable data.
Inter-rater agreement reveals whether the rating scale and criteria are actually well defined.
Human evaluation takes real time per query and does not scale to every query in a large set.
Comparing human ratings against automated scores reveals whether the automated metric tracks quality.
A small, representative sample is reviewed by humans, and its results generalize to the whole system.
